Getting started with VariPath

VariPath.Rmd

Code in this vignette is shown but not executed — the workflow needs a Perturb-seq Seurat object that is too large to ship with the package.

What problem this solves

A Perturb-seq experiment gives you, for every cell, both a perturbation label and a full transcriptome. The natural question — which biological pathways did each perturbation move? — is awkward to answer from principal components directly, because PCs are dense: almost every gene loads onto almost every component, so handing a PC’s gene list to an enrichment tool returns something vague.

VariPath applies a varimax rotation to the component space. Varimax redistributes variance so that each rotated component is loaded heavily by a smaller set of genes and near-zero by the rest. The subspace spanned is unchanged; what changes is interpretability. Sparser loadings mean a cleaner gene set per component, which means a sharper enrichment result — a better signal-to-noise ratio for perturbation-to-pathway association than the comparable methods we benchmarked against.

The pipeline is:

Seurat object (PCA run)
      │
      ├─ varimax-rotate the PC space           ──►  vari_weights
      ├─ fit perturbation ~ rotated component  ──►  fitted_models, fit_pvals_adj
      └─ enrichR on each component's top genes ──►  adjacency_table

Installation 

if (!require("devtools")) install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("ssobt/VariPath")

Dependencies are declared in DESCRIPTION, but a few — ggtree and aplot in particular — come from Bioconductor and may need installing by hand:

if (!require("BiocManager")) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("ggtree")
install.packages(c("enrichR", "aplot"))

A conda environment is recommended if you are managing several Bioconductor packages at once.

Input

You need a Seurat object that

  1. has PCA already run (Seurat::RunPCA()), and
  2. carries a metadata column identifying each cell’s perturbation.
library(Seurat)
library(VariPath)

# `adata` here is a Seurat object with a 'miR.family' column in its metadata
# giving the decoy / guide identity of each cell.
head(adata@meta.data[["miR.family"]])

Running the analysis 

out <- sc_varipath(
  seurat_obj          = adata,
  perturbation_column = "miR.family",
  enrichR_dbs         = "GO_Biological_Process_2021",
  loading_cutoff      = 0.1,
  FDR                 = 0.25
)

Arguments worth thinking about:

Argument Meaning
perturbation_column Metadata column holding each cell’s perturbation identity.
enrichR_dbs Which enrichR libraries to query. Multiple are allowed.
loading_cutoff How heavily a gene must load on a rotated component to be included in that component’s gene set. Raise it for stricter, smaller sets.
FDR Threshold for calling a perturbation-component association significant.

sc_varipath() returns a list:

Element Contents
vari_weights Varimax gene weights per rotated component.
fitted_models Linear models of perturbation against each component.
fit_pvals_adj Adjusted p-values for those associations.
perturbation_RC_df Tidy perturbation-to-component table, for plotting.
weights_dataframe Gene loadings, for plotting.
adjacency_table Top three associated pathways per component.

Save the result immediately. The object is expensive to recompute, and the plotting functions can exhaust memory on large datasets — losing the fit to an OOM part-way through plotting is an avoidable annoyance:

saveRDS(out, "varipath_out.rds")

Plotting

Two views, selected with plot_type:

# Which perturbations move which rotated components
plot_sc_varipath(out, plot_type = "perturbation")

# Which pathways each rotated component corresponds to
plot_sc_varipath(out, plot_type = "pathway")

Interpreting the output

A rotated component is not a pathway; it is an axis of coordinated expression that enriches for a pathway. Two practical consequences:

  • A perturbation can load onto several components. That is usually real — few perturbations affect exactly one coherent process — rather than a failure to converge.
  • Check the gene set, not just the pathway name. vari_weights is there so you can see which genes drove an enrichment call before you believe it. A component whose top loadings are ribosomal or mitochondrial genes is often reporting technical structure rather than biology.

Related work

VariPath came out of the Decoy-seq study, which screened regulatory small non-coding RNAs by Perturb-seq:

Choi B*, Sobti S*, Soto LM, Charbonneau T, Sababi A, Navickas A, Najafabadi HS, Goodarzi H. Decoy-seq unlocks scalable genetic screening for regulatory small noncoding RNAs. bioRxiv 2025. doi:10.1101/2025.01.25.634869

For quantifying heterogeneity rather than pathway shifts, see txnheterogeneity.
